# Book III, Proposition 5

*Circles cutting one another do not have the same centre*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument, with one step changed · one of our tacit rules already contains it (see Overlap)

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/05-idea.svg" alt="Give two circles that cut (red, blue) one centre, and the smaller (dashed) falls wholly within the larger, meeting it nowhere. Circles that cut never share a centre." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Give two circles that cut (red, blue) one centre, and the smaller (dashed) falls wholly within the larger, meeting it nowhere. Circles that cut never share a centre.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/05.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.5, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let the circles ABC, CDG cut one another at the points B, C;

I say that they will not have the same centre.

For, if possible, let it be E; let EC be joined, and let EFG be drawn through at random.

Then, since the point E is the centre of the circle ABC,

EC is equal to EF. [I. Def. 15]

Again, since the point E is the centre of the circle CDG,

EC is equal to EG.

But EC was proved equal to EF also;

therefore EF is also equal to EG, the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore the point E is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDG.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop05.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop05.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where several sentences share one step and where a step is argued another way; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Argued another way.** "therefore EF is also equal to EG, the less to the greater…" The Lean does not order F and G as the figure does: EF equal to EG makes ABC and CDG one circle (`circle_eq`), and the statement says they are two.
- **Carried together.** "Therefore the point E is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDG." The reductio's conclusion. The Lean supposed E the centre of both circles at the start and has reached the contradiction above, which proves it.

```lean
/-- If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre. -/
theorem Prop5 {E : Point} {ABC CDG : Circle} (hne : ABC ≠ CDG) (hcut : CirclesMeet ABC CDG) :
    ¬ (Centre E ABC ∧ Centre E CDG) := by
  -- For let the circles ABC, CDG cut one another at the points B, C;
  obtain ⟨B, C, -, -, -, hC_ABC, hC_CDG⟩ := hcut
  -- I say that they will not have the same centre.
  -- For, if possible, let it be E; let EC be joined, and let EFG be drawn through at random.
  rintro ⟨hE_ABC, hE_CDG⟩
  /- EC is drawn for the eye; Lean needs only its ends. An unlettered point
     chooses the direction of EFG, which meets both circles beyond E. -/
  obtain ⟨P, hP⟩ := exists_point [E]
  have hPE : P ≠ E := fun h => hP (h ▸ List.mem_singleton_self P)
  obtain ⟨EFG, hE_EFG, hP_EFG⟩ := Postulate1 E P hPE.symm
  obtain ⟨F, hF_ABC, -, -⟩ :=
    line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hE_ABC) hE_EFG hP_EFG hPE
  obtain ⟨G, hG_CDG, -, -⟩ :=
    line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hE_CDG) hE_EFG hP_EFG hPE
  -- Then, since the point E is the centre of the circle ABC,
  -- EC is equal to EF. [I. Def. 15]
  have hECF : ‖E C‖ = ‖E F‖ := Definition15 hE_ABC hC_ABC hF_ABC
  -- Again, since the point E is the centre of the circle CDG,
  -- EC is equal to EG.
  have hECG : ‖E C‖ = ‖E G‖ := Definition15 hE_CDG hC_CDG hG_CDG
  -- But EC was proved equal to EF also;
  -- therefore EF is also equal to EG, the less to the greater: which is impossible.
  have hEFG : ‖E F‖ = ‖E G‖ := hECF.symm.trans hECG
  /- Euclid sees F before G in the figure. We give the reason the supposed common centre
     cannot be: equal radii about one centre make one circle (System E, Diagram-segment 2),
     and ABC and CDG are two. -/
  exact hne (circle_eq hE_ABC hE_CDG hF_ABC hG_CDG hEFG)
  -- Therefore the point E is not the centre of the circles ABC, CDG.
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**What does the figure show?** Euclid supposes that the circles ABC and CDG, which cut one another at B and C, have one centre E, and lets EFG be drawn through at random. Then EF and EG are each equal to EC, and so to one another; yet in his figure F comes before G, and EF is the less. No figure can show two circles that cut and share a centre, so his shows us the supposition at the moment it fails.

**"Could be combined in one."** So Heath says of III.5 and III.6, and gives his reason: "It makes no difference whether the circles cut, or meet without cutting, so long as they do not coincide altogether; in either case they cannot have the same centre" (vol. 2, p. 12). He gives the combined enunciation, "*If the circumferences of two circles meet at a point they cannot have the same centre*", and turns it round: "*If two circles have the same centre and one point in their circumferences common, they must coincide altogether*" (vol. 2, p. 12).

**One centre and one point make one circle.** Heath's last sentence is a tacit rule in Lean, `circle_eq` (System E, Diagram-segment 2): a circle is fixed by its centre and its radius. So where Euclid sees F before G, Lean concludes from EF equal to EG that ABC and CDG are one circle. We therefore state that they are two, as Euclid's figure takes for granted: one circle taken twice meets itself everywhere and shares its own centre. The proof uses only C of the common points, so its argument proves Heath's combined enunciation as it stands, and III.6 goes the same way.

**The modern way.** A circle with centre E and radius r is the set of points at distance r from E. Two circles about E through C both have radius |EC| and are the same set: different circles about one centre never meet.

## Further reading

- For the combined enunciation Heath gives, that "circles which have the same centre and one point in their circumferences common, must coincide altogether", Isaac Todhunter's [*The Elements of Euclid*](https://archive.org/details/todhuntereuclid00todhrich) (1872, free online), his note on III.5 and III.6 (p. 272), which says they "should have been taken together" (also on [III.3](03.md)).
- For III.5 in red, yellow and blue, Nicholas Rougeux's [*Byrne's Euclid*](https://www.c82.net/euclid/) (2018, free online), where each coloured part lights up in the proof.
